title: La Dame de Fer (Eiffel Tower)
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover the Eiffel Tower in Paris: the visitor experience (three levels, restaurants such as Le Jules Verne, Gustave Eiffel's top-floor apartment), the democratizing effect of public access, Gustave Eiffel's background as an engineer and his financing of the tower through a public-private arrangement, the design competition and the collaboration with Maurice Koechlin, Émile Nouguier and Stephen Sauvestre, the choice of puddled wrought iron, construction from 1887 to 1889 with heated riveting and one worker death, opening for the 1889 World's Fair, the artists' Petition of the Three Hundred and Maupassant's criticism, Eiffel's defense of the tower, wind-pressure-based shape, the planned 20-year lifespan and how radio use saved it, its World War II history, the paint cycle and "Eiffel Tower brown," lighting and electricity costs, and the elevators. The episode ends with New Year's wishes and a listener mail about pet turkeys.
topics: Guy de Maupassant Eiffel Tower criticism

segments.title: Opening banter and visitor impressions
segments.summary: The hosts open with personal stories about visiting the Eiffel Tower, Chuck's fear of heights, the stairs, the tourist crowds, and the three levels.

segments.title: Restaurants, Eiffel's apartment, and democratizing access
segments.summary: They discuss the Jules Verne restaurant and its prices, Gustave Eiffel's top-floor apartment, and how public access made Paris views available to non-wealthy visitors.

segments.title: Gustave Eiffel the engineer and iron
segments.summary: Eiffel's background as an engineer rather than an architect, his railroad bridges, and his preference for puddled wrought iron over steel.

segments.title: Financing and the public-private deal
segments.summary: Eiffel financed the tower through share issues, with a state seed grant and a twenty-year concession on admissions and concessions, and his shareholders profited.

segments.title: Design competition and collaborators
segments.summary: The design competition for the 1889 fair, the rival stone proposal by Jules Bourdais, and the initial design by Koechlin and Nouguier refined by architect Stephen Sauvestre; Eiffel bought the designs from his employees.

segments.title: Twenty-year lifespan and World's Fair tradition
segments.summary: The original plan was for the tower to stand only twenty years and be dismantled, consistent with World's Fair structures, which were often torn down.

segments.title: Construction, riveting, and safety
segments.summary: Construction from January 1887 with the tower started in July, components made at a workshop six kilometers away, heated rivets hammered on site, tenth-of-a-millimeter precision, one worker death, and Eiffel's oversight.

segments.title: Opening and the artists' petition
segments.summary: The tower opened after the fair began, with the first visitors climbing stairs. Artists signed the Petition of the Three Hundred against it; Maupassant criticized it, and Eiffel defended its beauty.

segments.title: Wind-shaped design and strength
segments.summary: The tower's taper was calculated from wind pressure, its load strength, and Eiffel's public responsibility statement.

segments.title: Radio saves the tower and World War II
segments.summary: Radio experiments and a permanent radio installation gave the tower military and communications value, saving it from demolition. During WWII, the resistance cut the elevator cables and a dogfight occurred beneath the tower; Hitler's order to demolish Paris monuments was not carried out by von Choltitz.

segments.title: Paint, lighting, electricity, and elevators
segments.summary: The tower is repainted on a seven-year cycle, with the color 'Eiffel Tower brown' and an ombre shading; lighting and electricity costs; and the hydraulic elevators, Otis's 1889 demonstration, and beef fat grease.

segments.title: Fact-checking the list and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts question the five billion lights and the cost figures from an online list, which they trace to Live Science, then close with fun facts and a New Year's greeting.

segments.title: Listener mail: pet turkeys
segments.summary: A listener writes about pet domestic turkeys and their personalities.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and sign off.
